extracted.intended_audience: naturalists/anthropologists and scientifically literate readers evaluating species vs varieties (application to human races)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations used by naturalists to decide whether allied forms (here, human races) should be ranked as distinct species or as varieties, with application to anthropological and comparative-anatomical evidence. Covers morphological, physiological, reproductive, geographic and historical lines of evidence and their limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of difference between forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of difference between them, and whether such differences relate to few or many points of structure, and whether they are of physiological importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalists weigh both the magnitude and the breadth of differences: many small differences across many parts, or differences of physiological significance, count more toward specific rank than a single trivial difference. Examples cited include differences in hair texture, body proportions, lung capacity, skull form, and brain convolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Constancy of character is what is chiefly valued and sought for by naturalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If forms have retained the same characters for a long period, this is strong evidence for treating them as species. Persistence through centuries (e.g., likeness to ancient Egyptian figures) strengthens the specific interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterility or reduced fertility between crossed forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a slight degree of sterility between any two forms when first crossed, or in their offspring, is generally considered as a decisive test of their specific distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes many caveats: sterility varies widely, can be affected by conditions of life and domestication, and is governed by complex laws (unequal fertility of converse crosses, effects of habituation). Thus sterility, while important, is not an absolute or infallible criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence without blending (absence of intermediate varieties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independently of fusion from intercrossing, the complete absence, in a well-investigated region, of varieties linking together any two closely-allied forms is probably the most important of all the criterions of their specific distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from mere constancy because even highly variable forms may not yield intermediate varieties; if no intermediates are found across a well-sampled area, that argues for species status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical distribution (zoological province congruence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical distribution is often brought into play; forms living in widely separated areas, in which most other inhabitants are specifically distinct, are usually looked at as distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cautions this is not decisive but notes that the different races of man are distributed over the world in much the same zoological provinces as distinct mammal species (e.g., Australian, Mongolian, Negro, Papuan vs Malay divisions), which can be taken as supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of external parasites
rubrics_metrics.description: If external parasites collected from different human races appear to be specifically distinct, this may be urged as an argument that the races themselves ought to be classed as distinct species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mr. Murray's work finding distinct Pediculi (lice) types on different races, with constant differences in many specimens; anecdote that lice from Sandwich Islanders died off English sailors — parasite specificity is treated as meaningful corroborative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of mutual fertility in practice (empirical fertility data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observations on whether races when crossed are fertile together, and the vitality/fecundity of the mixed offspring, bear on specific distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites Broca and other observers with mixed results (some races fertile together, some alleged sterility reports disproved). He notes social factors, mortality, and sample biases (e.g., degraded social status of mixed groups) can confound apparent fertility rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of offspring from crosses (blend vs parental resemblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the offspring from a cross are blended/intermediate or whether some offspring resemble one parent and others the other parent has been used as an indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is unreliable as a general rule: ordinary result often intermediate, but sometimes offspring variably resemble parents (especially when differences arose as sudden variations or monstrosities). Observational examples include varying appearances among negro × other-race offspring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of variability of purported distinguishing characters
rubrics_metrics.description: If the distinctive characters of a putative race are highly variable, this undermines the sense that the group is a distinct species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes many races show high internal variation (e.g., negro slaves in Brazil, Polynesians), and that 'no character can be named which is distinctive of a race and is constant' in many cases; high intraspecific variability argues against separate species rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to different climates and constitutional/mental differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in adaptation to widely different climates, constitution, liability to diseases, and distinct mental/emotional characteristics are considered when assessing distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such ecological and physiological differences can support specific distinction (e.g., races adapted to Arctic vs tropical), but must be weighed with other criteria; mental/emotional traits are observed but are less clear-cut for taxonomic rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal persistence (historical continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retention of the same character for many centuries (historical/archaeological continuity) is taken as evidence toward species-level distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: apparent similarity of some modern races to types represented in Egyptian monuments dated ~4000 years ago is used to argue long-term constancy; caveats include interpretive ambiguity of ancient representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphometric and anatomical measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed measurements and anatomical differences (texture of hair, relative proportions of body parts, capacity of lungs, skull form and capacity, convolutions of the brain) are indicators of difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites large data sets (military/anthropological statistics, museum collections) as the empirical basis; such morphometric evidence must be evaluated for constancy and degree across populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to inhabit same area without fusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether forms remain distinct when mingled together in large numbers in the same country (resist fusion) is an important practical test of specific distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin observes widespread fusion (e.g., Brazil, Chiloe, Pacific islands, Fiji, parts of Africa), arguing that races are often not sufficiently distinct to maintain separation in sympatry; lack of fusion argues for species status, frequent fusion argues against it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution regarding sterility as an acquired vs incidental trait (domestication effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sterility of crossed species is not a specially-acquired quality by selection but is often incidental on other acquired differences; domestication tends to eliminate sterility between forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin explains that sterility can be modified by conditions and habituation; since sterililty can arise incidentally and may be mitigated by domestication, it should not be treated as an absolute determinant of species status.
